translate.output: Then does the meaning of freedom ultimately not apply to the individual? One says: How evil are these words! The freedom of the group is the accumulation of individual freedom. A person cannot leave the group and survive on their own; if the group does not protect its freedom, then another group will invade from outside, oppress it, and seize it — then what becomes of individual freedom? With my shallow learning, wanting to clarify this with my meagre words — how could I know if it is possible? … Are there those in the world who love freedom? They must be careful not to poison freedom and thereby poison the world.
translate.gold: In that case, can freedom after all not be applied to the individual? I answer: nonsense, what talk is this? Collective freedom is the sum of individual freedoms. People cannot survive on their own apart from the group. If the group does not protect its freedom, then other groups will come from outside to invade it, oppress it and plunder it, and then what will be left of the individual's freedom? For one of shallow learning like me to try to explain it in a few paltry words: how can I know that it will do? … Are there people in the world who love freedom? Let them take care not to poison freedom, and thereby poison the world.

translate.output: On the 23rd day of the 4th month of the 24th year of Guangxu, the Grand Council received an imperial edict: For several years, officials at home and abroad have discussed current affairs, mostly advocating reform to strengthen the country. Recently, several edicts have been issued — such as opening a special examination, disbanding supernumerary troops, revising the military examination system, and establishing primary and secondary schools — all carefully deliberated and fully prepared, only just ready for implementation. However, the prevailing mood has not yet fully opened; opinions are not unanimous. Some, claiming to be elder statesmen worried for the country, argue that the old statutes must be rigidly kept and the new methods must be rejected. Many voices clamor, but empty words are of no help. One may ask: given today's situation and the state of the nation, if we still rely on untrained troops, limited funds, scholars without practical learning, and craftsmen without good teachers, with such disparity in strength and wealth, can we really hope to wield a stick to beat troops in strong armor and sharp weapons? ... The Capital University is the model for all provinces and should be undertaken first. The Grand Councilors and the princes and ministers of the Office for General Management of Affairs Concerning the Various Countries are ordered to confer and memorialize promptly and properly. ... Let this be circulated to all for their information. Respectfully.
translate.gold: On the 23rd day of the 4th month of the 24th year of Guangxu, the Grand Secretariat received the following edict: For several years now, officials at court and in the provinces have studied current affairs, and most have advocated reform and self-strengthening. Recently edicts have been issued one after another: setting up a special examination, cutting surplus troops, reforming the military examinations, establishing schools of all levels. All were examined again and again and planned most thoroughly, and it has only just been proposed to put them into effect. But attitudes are not yet open, and opinions cannot agree. Some take cover behind experience and concern for the country, holding that the old institutions must be held fast and the new methods rejected. Many mouths clamour, but empty words are of no help. Let us ask: with the situation as it is today, and the state's strength as it is, if we still rely on untrained troops and limited funds, with scholars lacking practical learning and artisans lacking good teachers, the strong and the weak set side by side, the rich and the poor so far apart, can we really make clubs to beat strong armour and sharp weapons? … The Imperial University in the capital is to be an example to the provinces and above all should be set up first. Let the Grand Councillors and the princes and ministers of the Zongli Yamen deliberate on it jointly and report properly and quickly by memorial. … Let this be proclaimed to all. Respect this.

Minister of the Interior Cheng Dequan submits this report. I observe that protecting the people and defending the country depend on police administration as the pivot of government; selecting the worthy and employing the capable depend on schools as the reservoir of talent. Nanjing is now the model capital; all police matters must first be concretely reformed so as to set an example for the provinces. However, since the Ministry was just established, funds are difficult; all expenditures should strive for economy. Therefore the existing Jiangsu Higher Police Academy is renamed the Ministry of the Interior Police School. First, 240 trainee policemen from the Training Institute are recruited and taught in separate departments, as an urgent measure to treat the symptoms. As for regular students, they will be recruited, examined, and educated only after reliable funds are secured, to fulfill the Great President's original intention of seeking the people's happiness. At the same time, the Ministry's Police Bureau Director Sun Runyu is appointed concurrently as Police School Principal, to ensure swift implementation, so that both public and private interests benefit. The reasons for opening the Police School should properly be stated in a document and submitted for your review and action. This is submitted.

According to the petition: the land on the west bank of Shaobo Lake has long lain fallow; the representatives cannot bear to waste its profit and plan to reclaim and cultivate it, which truly cannot be delayed. However, the total area of that bank must be calculated in mu and mapped, and first submitted to the Ministry, so that the Yangzhou Civil Governor can be ordered to verify it. The representatives are to comply immediately and also draw up proper stock-subscription regulations and methods, and submit them together to the Ministry. This endorsement.
translate.gold: Cheng Dequan, Minister of the Interior, reports as follows. I humbly consider that for protecting the people and defending the state, police affairs are the key to administration; and for choosing the worthy and employing the able, schools are the place where talent is gathered. I note that Nanjing is now the capital, and all police matters must first be thoroughly reformed before it can serve as a model for the provinces. But this ministry has only just been founded and funds are difficult, so all measures should, it seems, be as economical as possible. I have therefore converted the existing Jiangnan Higher Police School into the Ministry of the Interior Police School. It will first recruit 240 police cadets for the training institute and teach them by subject, as an emergency measure. As for students of the regular course, as soon as definite funds have been raised, they will be admitted by examination and educated, so as to fulfil the President's intention of working to advance the people's happiness. I have also at once appointed Sun Runyu, head of this ministry's police bureau, as principal of the police school concurrently, in the hope of setting it up quickly, so that both public and private interests may benefit. As to the opening of the police school, it is proper to prepare this document and request you to examine it and put it into effect. This petition is necessary. According to your petition, the land on the west shore of Lake Shaobo has long lain waste, and you representatives cannot bear to leave its profit in the ground and plan to reclaim and cultivate it. This truly cannot be delayed. But you should measure in mu how much land there is on that shore, draw a map and first submit them to the ministry, so that we can pass them on with an order to the civil governor of Yangzhou to verify. You representatives are directed to comply at once, and also to draw up proper regulations and procedures for raising capital, and submit them to the ministry together. This is the ruling.

translate.output: Article One: The treaty previously settled at Jiangning on the twenty-fourth day of the seventh month of the preceding renyin year shall continue to be observed. The old post-war settlement treaty concluded at Guangdong and the existing trade regulations, now being revised, have already been incorporated into the new treaty; therefore all the old treaties are to be treated as waste paper. Article Fifty: Henceforth all British documents shall be written in English characters; for the time being Chinese texts shall still be supplied alongside them, but once China selects and dispatches students to study English and they become proficient in the language, the Chinese versions shall no longer be supplied. From now on, wherever there is a dispute over wording, the English text shall be taken as the authoritative version. In this treaty negotiation the Chinese and English texts have been carefully compared and found to be without error; the same principle shall apply. Article Fifty-one: Henceforth in all kinds of official documents, whether in the capital or in the provinces, when referring to British officials and people, the character 'yi' (barbarian) must not be used.
translate.gold: Article 1: The peace treaty concluded earlier at Jiangning on the 24th day of the 7th month of the renyin year remains in force. The supplementary treaty concluded in Guangdong and the trade regulations are now revised; since they have been incorporated into the new treaty, all the old treaties are null and void. Article 50: From now on, British communications shall all be written in English. For the time being they will still be accompanied by Chinese; as soon as China has selected and sent students to learn English and they are proficient in the language, Chinese will no longer be sent with them. From now on, whenever there is a dispute about wording, the English shall in all cases be taken as the correct meaning. The treaty now concluded, of which the Chinese and English texts have been carefully checked and found without error, is also subject to this rule. Article 51: From now on, in official documents of all kinds, whether in the capital or the provinces, the character 夷 may not, of course, be written in referring to British officials and subjects.

translate.output: Hè Xūlí sits alone in a single room, in the south of England, with mountains at his back and open fields before him; the scenes beyond the railing are all clearly spread out as if under his hand. He then lets his imagination travel back two thousand years, to the time before the Roman general Caesar had arrived here, and wonders what the scenery was like at that time. … Therefore one knows that the saying ‘nothing changes’ is decidedly not the way of Heaven. The principle by which things endure for ages actually lies within constant, unceasing change. What one sees at present may change after twenty or thirty years, and it may also change after twenty or thirty thousand years. One merely projects the past into the future and sees that change is only beginning, with no known limit. Nevertheless, although the course of Heaven changes, there is something unchanging that operates within it. What is this unchanging thing? It is called ‘Heavenly Evolution’ (tiān yǎn). Taking Heavenly Evolution as the substance, its function has two aspects: ‘struggle of things’ (wù jìng) and ‘Heavenly selection’ (tiān zé). All things are like this, but it is especially evident among living beings. ‘Struggle of things’ means things strive to preserve themselves. One thing contends with all other things; some survive, some perish, and the result returns to Heavenly selection. ‘Heavenly selection’ means that amid the struggle, only one survives. That which survives must have its reason for surviving: it must be the endowment it received from Heaven, its own developed ability, the time and place it encounters, and all the material forces outside its own body — these mutually plan and blend together. Only then does it alone escape extinction and stand on its own. Viewed from its effect, it appears as if this thing was specially favoured by Heaven and selected to survive; this is what is called Heavenly selection. Heavenly selection is selection by nature; although it selects, there is no selector, just as the struggle of things has no conscious striving, yet it is the utmost striving under Heaven. Spencer said: ‘Heavenly selection means preserving the most suitable.’ Once things have struggled to survive, Heaven then selects from the aftermath of their struggle; one struggle, one selection, and the process of transformation emerges.
translate.gold: Huxley is sitting alone in a room in the south of England, with hills behind and fields in front; the scenes beyond the railing are as clear as if they lay below his desk. He then imagines what this place looked like two thousand years ago, before the Roman general Caesar came. …… Hence we know that "unchanging" is by no means the way of heaven's course, and that the principle by which things endure and take shape lies, on the contrary, in ceaseless change. What we see before us may well be transformed in twenty or thirty years, or again in twenty or thirty thousand. It is only that, inferring the future from past events, change has far still to run, and we do not know where it will end. And yet, though heaven's course changes, something unchanging operates within it. What is this unchanging thing? It is called evolution (天演). Evolution is the substance, and it has two functions: the struggle of things (物競) and the selection of heaven (天擇). This is so of all things, and most evident among living things. The struggle of things is things striving to preserve themselves. When one thing contends with thing after thing, it either survives or perishes, and the result comes down to the selection of heaven. The selection of heaven is when things contend and one alone survives. Then there must be a reason for its survival: its endowment from heaven, the abilities it attains by itself, the time and place it meets with, and all the forces of things outside its body must have worked together and complemented one another. Only then does it alone escape perishing and become able to stand on its own. And looking at it from the result, it is as if this thing had been specially favoured by heaven and selected to survive: this is what is called the selection of heaven. The selection of heaven is selection by nature: it selects, yet no one selects; just as the struggle of things seems to be no struggle, and is in truth the fiercest struggle in the world. Spencer said: "The selection of heaven is the preservation of the fittest." Since things struggle to survive, and heaven then selects among them after their struggle, with each struggle and each selection, change comes about.

punctuate.output: 中國政治與文化之變革，莫劇於殷周之際。殷周間之大變革，自其表言之，不過一姓一家之興亡與都邑之移轉；自其裏言之，則舊制度廢而新制度興，舊文化廢而新文化興。又自其表言之，則古聖人之所以取天下及所以守之者，若無以異於後世之帝王；而自其裏言之，則其制度文物與其立制之本意，乃出於萬世治安之大計，其心術與規摹，迥非後世帝王所能夢見也。欲觀周之所以定天下，必自其制度始矣。周人制度之大異於商者：一曰立子立嫡之制，由是而生宗法及喪服之制，並由是而有封建子弟之制、君天子臣諸侯之制；二曰廟數之制；三曰同姓不婚之制。此數者皆周之所以綱紀天下，其旨則在納上下於道德，而合天子、諸侯、卿大夫、士庶民以成一道德之團體。周公制作之本意，實在於此。此非穿鑿附會之言也。茲篇所論，皆有事實爲之根據。試略述之：其條例則《春秋左氏傳》之說曰：「太子死，有母弟則立之；無則立長；年鈞擇賢；義鈞則卜。」《公羊》家之說曰：「禮，嫡夫人無子，立右媵；右媵無子，立左媵。」此二說中，後說尤爲詳密。顧皆後儒充類之說，當立法之初，未必窮其變至此。然所謂「立子以貴不以長，立適以長不以賢」者，乃傳子法之精髓。當時雖未必有此語，固已用此意矣。

translate.output: The transformation of Chinese politics and culture was never more drastic than at the transition from Yin to Zhou. ... The great transformation between Yin and Zhou, viewed from the surface, was merely the rise and fall of one surname and one clan and the transfer of the capital; viewed from the inside, the old institutions were abolished and new institutions arose, the old culture was abolished and new culture arose. Again, viewed from the surface, the way the ancient sages gained the empire and the way they held it seemed no different from later emperors; but viewed from the inside, their institutions, cultural artifacts, and the original intent behind establishing those institutions came from a grand plan for the peace and order of ten thousand generations — their principles and models were utterly beyond what later emperors could even dream of. To understand how Zhou settled the empire, one must start with its institutions. The great differences between Zhou institutions and those of Shang were three: first, the system of establishing the heir and establishing the legitimate son; from this arose the clan-law system and the mourning-attire system, and also from this arose the system of enfeoffing younger brothers and the system of the Son of Heaven as lord over the feudal lords; second, the system of the number of ancestral temples; third, the system prohibiting marriage between persons of the same surname. These several items were all the means by which Zhou disciplined the empire. Their aim was to bring superiors and inferiors into morality, and to unite the Son of Heaven, feudal lords, ministers, grandees, officers, and commoners into a single moral community. This was the true original intent of the Duke of Zhou's creation of institutions. This is not forced or far-fetched interpretation; what this essay discusses all has factual basis. I will briefly set it forth. ... As for the specific provisions, the account in the *Spring and Autumn Annals: Zuo Commentary* says: 'When the heir apparent dies, if there is a younger brother by the same mother, establish him; if not, establish the eldest. If their ages are equal, choose the worthy; if their worth is equal, then divine.' The Gongyang school's account says: 'According to ritual, if the principal wife has no son, establish the son of the right-hand secondary wife; if the right-hand secondary wife has no son, establish the son of the left-hand secondary wife...' Between these two accounts, the latter is especially detailed and precise. However, both are later scholars' analogical extensions; at the time the legislation was first enacted, it may not have exhausted all variations to this extent. Yet the saying "establish the son by nobility not by age, establish the legitimate heir by age not by worth" is the essence of the law of succession; although that exact wording may not have existed at the time, the intent was already being put into practice.
translate.gold: Of all the changes in China's government and culture, none is more drastic than that at the transition from Shang to Zhou. …… The great change between Shang and Zhou, seen from the surface, was no more than the rise and fall of one family and the moving of the capital; seen from within, old institutions fell and new institutions arose, old culture fell and new culture arose. Again, seen from the surface, the ways in which the ancient sages won the empire and kept it seem no different from those of later emperors; but seen from within, their institutions, their culture and their original intention in founding the institutions came in fact from a grand plan for order and peace for ten thousand generations, and their thinking and design were far beyond anything later emperors could dream of. If one wishes to see how the Zhou settled the empire, one must begin from its institutions. The Zhou institutions that differ greatly from the Shang are, first, the institution of succession by the son and by the son of the principal wife, from which arose the lineage system and the mourning system, and from which came the enfeoffment of sons and younger brothers and the system in which the Son of Heaven is lord and the feudal lords are subjects; second, the number of ancestral temples; third, the rule that those of the same surname do not marry. These are all the means by which the Zhou gave order to the empire. Their purpose was to bring high and low within morality, and to unite the Son of Heaven, the feudal lords, ministers, great officers, gentlemen and the common people into one moral community. The Duke of Zhou's original intention in making institutions truly lay here. These are not far-fetched or forced words: everything this essay argues has facts as its evidence. Let me set it out briefly. …… The rules are given in the account of the *Zuo Commentary*: "When the heir dies, if there is a younger brother by the same mother, he is made heir; if not, the eldest is made heir. If they are equal in age, the worthiest is chosen; if equal in merit, the matter is divined." The Gongyang school's account says: "By the rites, if the principal wife has no son, the son of the right secondary wife is made heir; if the right secondary wife has no son, the son of the left secondary wife is made heir; ……" Of these two accounts, the latter is especially detailed, but both are the extrapolations of later Confucians; when the rule was first laid down, its makers did not necessarily work out every case in this way. Yet what is called "a son is made heir by rank, not by age; the son of the principal wife is made heir by age, not by worth" is the essence of the rule of succession by sons; though these words may not have been said at the time, the idea was certainly already in use.

translate.output: I previously formed a friendship with your elder brother Jifang, and thus heard of your virtue, Yuanfang, longing for a meeting. Yesterday in the provincial capital I chanced upon you and found that your talent and bearing surpass what I had heard. I only regret that we met so late, and unexpectedly we parted after a single night, which again makes me regret how quickly we separated. After parting, I reached Tianjin on the fourth day, and went to Pingshu on the tenth; the moon has not yet completed a full cycle, yet I have changed locations twice. Traveling wearily through wind and dust, all for the scholar's livelihood — I both pity and laugh at myself. Recently my colleagues returned home, leaving me alone in the lodging; with the clear chime and red fish, it is just like practicing in an ancient temple. As the west wind blows and yellow leaves fall, my thoughts of returning grow frequent; I trust your letter (the double carp) will not fail to reach me. Has your health recovered? Official duties are many and burdensome; you must take good care of yourself. Sending my thoughts on the wind, I cannot express all I feel. I have not seen the green wu-trees and emerald bamboos for a long time; whenever the moon is bright and the wind clear, my spirit yearns deeply. I also wonder why you have not been on duty for so long. Recently I received a letter from Ruan Xihou, learning that you have been traveling in Shandong, and that your lotus-planting at Qiu has not been just a day's work. The green duckweed forming a green mat — everywhere it is eagerly bought — is only natural. Your younger brother's talent and spirit, I thought him a lone crane on Ji Mountain, enough to outshine a flock of chickens; how unexpected that the jade lute should be shattered, and the grave grass already grown thick — it fills one with sorrow and regret! I first stayed as a guest in Liaoxi, then toured the Tianjin marshes. This spring I again had the journey to Pingshu. Year after year I rush to meet deadlines, still just a hired hand; the reason is that the village girl's moth-eyebrows are hard to please in this age.
translate.gold: I, your younger brother, formerly had the good fortune to make friends with your younger brother, and so heard of your worth as the elder, and longed for the pleasure of meeting you. Yesterday I met you by chance in the provincial capital, and felt that your talent and bearing surpassed even what I had heard. Just as I was regretting that we had not met sooner, we unexpectedly parted after a single night, and now I regret that we were separated so soon. After we parted, I reached Tianjin on the fourth and went to Pingshu on the tenth: in less than a month I have changed place twice. Travel-worn, I do nothing but weed other people's fields; I pity myself, and can also laugh at myself. Just now my colleagues have gone home, and I live alone in the office; add the clear chime and the red wooden fish, and it is just like an old temple for religious practice. With the west wind and the yellow leaves, I often long for you deeply; you will surely not abandon me, but will send me a letter. Have you recovered your health? With the wedding arrangements so many and tiring, please take good care of yourself. I send my thoughts by the wind, and cannot express all I feel. I have long not seen your bearing, like green parasol trees and jade bamboo; whenever the moon is bright and the wind clear, I long for you in spirit. I had wondered why you had not been on duty for so long. Recently I received a letter from Ruan Xihou and learnt that you have travelled to Shandong and have long been serving in a secretariat at Chuqiu. Fine swords and fine jade are sought after everywhere: that is only to be expected. Your younger brother's talent and spirit, I was sure, like Ji Shao, the lone crane, would shine among the flock of chickens. Who could have expected that Boya's zither would be broken, and that the grass on the grave is already a year old? It moves one to sorrow! I, your younger brother, first lived in Liaoxi, then soon moved to Tianjin and its lakes. This spring I have again taken up a post at Pingshu. Year after year I sew for others, still a hired hand: truly because a village girl's fine eyebrows are hard for the age to admire.
